title: Make housing a fundamental constitutional right
detail: A constitutional reform so housing becomes a fundamental right (*derecho fundamental*) that citizens can enforce against the authorities. The programme does not set out the voting procedure.
c: Moving the right to housing from the guiding principles (art. 47) into the fundamental rights section needs the art. 168 procedure: two-thirds of both chambers, dissolution of parliament, a new vote and a referendum. Impossible without PP, which opposes it.

s.t: Spanish Constitution, art. 47 (BOE)
Spanish Constitution, art. 168 (BOE)

title: CASA 47: a public stock of 100,000 homes
detail: The state housing agency CASA 47 (set up in late 2025) would build and buy 100,000 homes to sell or rent long-term at affordable prices, on top of regional and municipal housing. Income is reinvested, and public land goes into a land bank for social operators and housing co-ops.
c: The agency exists, but 100,000 homes (about a full year of national output: 100,980 in 2024) in one term is optimistic. Existing public land and SAREB homes would come first; new building takes years.
pos: A permanent affordable rental stock on the Vienna and Basque model holds down prices in the long run and never returns to the open market.
neg: 100,000 homes is about 0.5% of main homes (around 19.7 million households, INE): a small, slow effect on prices overall. Buying finished homes competes with buyers and can push prices up.

s.t: Housing Ministry: Observatorio de Vivienda y Suelo, annual bulletin 2024 (La Moncloa)
INE: population and households at 1 Jan 2026 (ECP)

title: Freeze rents above the official reference index
detail: Temporarily freeze rents above the reference price index (*índice de referencia*) in stressed markets. No limit or formula is given. The Housing Ministry would publish its own map of stressed areas (*zonas tensionadas*), which under the 2023 Housing Law the regions should draw up but often do not.
c: The Housing Law already allows rent limits, but only where a region has declared a stressed area, and PP-run regions do not. No formula is given. Studies of Catalonia find rents 4–6% lower but disagree on whether supply shrank.
pos: Protects tenants from sharp rises in the most stressed cities.
neg: Caps restrain prices: studies of Catalonia find rents 4–6% lower. But one of them sees pricier homes leaving the market, and after the 2024 caps rental listings fell by about 20% (Fedea estimate). In Berlin, rents just outside the city rose sharply.

s.t: Ley 12/2023 on the right to housing (BOE)

title: Tax on "vulture funds" and large landlords
detail: A progressive tax on homes owned by large landlords (*grandes tenedores*) and funds (*fondos buitre*) unless let as affordable long-term rentals. It would hit homes used as tourist lets, left empty or let at "excessive" rents. Thresholds and rates are not given.
c: The tax needs an ordinary law, but also a majority (Junts is against). PP-run regions can zero out similar taxes at their level, and there is a risk of challenges for double taxation.
pos: An incentive to let or sell empty homes, and money for housing policy.
neg: Funds own only a few per cent of the housing stock; some of the tax will be passed on to tenants, and investors may pull out of build-to-rent.

title: TU CASA: interest-free loans of up to €50,000 for a first home
detail: A €10 billion credit line offering interest-free loans of up to €50,000 to buy a first home (*primera vivienda*), for people with stable income but no savings. The limit would be raised if the money runs out. Income criteria are not given.
c: €10 billion through the state bank ICO is realistic as a credit line. But a 0% loan for the deposit boosts demand while supply is short, and will raise prices.
pos: The interest-free loan replaces missing savings, making a first home easier to buy for young people.
neg: More demand without new supply means higher prices. The state carries the risk of unpaid loans.

title: Raise tax on large capital income to 35%
detail: The first two savings-income (*rentas del ahorro*) bands stay at 19% up to €6,000 and 21% up to €50,000; above that rates rise step by step to 35% on capital income over €300,000 (currently 30% at that level).
c: A technically simple change to income tax. But it needs a majority in Congress, which PSOE often lacked in the last term. Capital is mobile: some income will move into lower-taxed structures.
pos: Fairer: wealthy people's capital income would be taxed almost like wages.
neg: Capital is mobile: some will move abroad or into holding companies, so revenue may fall short of expectations.

title: Refundable child tax credit
detail: Turn the tax-free child allowance (*mínimo por descendiente*) into a refundable tax credit, so that about 2 million low- and middle-income families who file no return or owe no tax can use it.
c: Technically simple; the mechanism already exists for mothers of children under 3. The cost is moderate, in our estimate a few hundred million to €1 billion.
pos: Money for low-income families who cannot use the allowance today: an effective measure against child poverty.
neg: Costs up to about €1 billion a year; paid as a monthly advance, it risks overpayments and later clawbacks.

s.t: Ley 35/2006 on income tax, maternity deduction (BOE)

title: Write inflation-linked pensions into the Constitution
detail: Put protection of the public pension system and its indexation to consumer prices (*IPC*) into the Constitution. Today indexation is guaranteed by an ordinary law.
c: A constitutional amendment under art. 167 needs three-fifths of both chambers (210 deputies) and is out of reach without PP. PP supports indexation to the CPI, so agreement on substance is possible, but politically unlikely.

s.t: Spanish Constitution, art. 167 (BOE)

title: By law, minimum wage at no less than 60% of the average wage
detail: Set in law that the minimum wage (*SMI*) cannot fall below 60% of the average wage, updated for prices, wages and productivity, and that rises cannot be swallowed by absorbing bonuses (*absorción de complementos*). The SMI is €1,221 today.
c: The SMI already sits near the 60% target (€1,221 × 14 payments in 2026). Writing it into law is realistic. Critics note that in poorer regions the bar is higher.
pos: Protects the purchasing power of low earners and reduces in-work poverty.
neg: In poorer regions and small businesses, 60% of the national average wage is a high bar: a risk of lost jobs or a shift to the informal economy.

s.t: Real Decreto 126/2026: 2026 minimum wage of €1,221 a month (BOE)

title: 37.5-hour working week with no pay cut
detail: Complete the cut in the working week to 37.5 hours and encourage collective agreements to reach 35, without loss of pay, with a timetable through social dialogue and transition periods for small firms (*pymes*). No date is given.
c: Congress sent the 37.5-hour bill back to the government on 10 Sep 2025 (amendments by PP, Vox and Junts). It could only pass with a different balance of seats; the employers' federation CEOE is against.

s.t: Congress, BOCG 15-A-58-3: 37.5-hour bill returned to the government (10 Sep 2025)

title: *Autónomos*: contributions based on real income
detail: Update the self-employment statute (*Estatuto del Trabajo Autónomo*), keep moving to contributions based on real income (*cotización por ingresos reales*), and make the self-employed jobless benefit (*cese de actividad*) easier to claim. Contribution amounts are not given.
c: Contributions based on real income are already being phased in from 2023 to 2032. Continuing is realistic.
pos: Fairer contributions: low earners pay less, high earners more.
neg: Higher-earning *autónomos* will pay more; harder for people with uneven income.

s.t: Real Decreto-ley 13/2022: self-employed contributions and flat rate (BOE)

title: End waiting lists: about 7% of GDP for public health
detail: Lock in public health spending at around 7% of GDP, strengthen the public National Health System (*SNS*) and gradually raise prevention spending to the European average. No timetable or euro amount.
c: Public health spending is already about 6.5–7% of GDP, so the figure is nearly met. Waiting lists depend on the regions and the shortage of doctors, not on a share of GDP.
pos: Stable health funding and shorter waits.
neg: Regions run the system and may simply replace their own money with state money; no funding source is named.

s.t: Eurostat, gov_10a_exp: Spain's public health spending, % of GDP (2022–2024)

title: State takes on €83 billion of regional debt
detail: Partial takeover (*asunción parcial*) of €83 billion of regional debt (*deuda autonómica*) to ease regional finances. Shares and conditions are not given.
c: The government sent a bill to write off €83 billion to parliament in December 2025. It is an organic law (176 votes); Junts has doubts and PP-run regions refuse, seeing it as a concession to ERC. State debt rises by the same amount.
pos: Heavily indebted regions (Catalonia, Valencia, Andalusia) get room to spend on services.
neg: Moral hazard: regions that borrowed more gain more. The debt does not vanish; it moves to the state.

s.t: Finance Ministry, 9 Dec 2025: bill to write off €83,252 million of regional debt sent to parliament
Spanish Constitution, art. 81 (BOE)

title: Keep the nuclear phase-out by 2035
detail: Keep the current timetable for closing nuclear plants (*calendario de cierre nuclear*) by 2035 and fund "just transition" projects in affected areas. No new plants.
c: The timetable can be kept, but Almaraz has already been extended to 2030 at its owners' request. Closing 7 GW without replacement baseload would, in our estimate, raise prices and reliance on gas.
pos: No new nuclear waste, and more room on the grid for renewables.
neg: About a fifth of output (19% in 2025, REE), stable and emission-free, disappears: a risk of higher prices and emissions if the replacement (storage, grids, gas) is not ready.

s.t: Orden TED/864/2026: Almaraz extended to 8 June 2030 (BOE)
